summary: Earth Analogs Explorer is a free web tool that finds the places on Earth most like any chosen point on the Moon or Mars, and shows where Earth has no match at all. Teams test rovers, landers, instruments and procedures at Earth analog sites, but those sites are often chosen by tradition or access. We choose them by measurement. We score every 1° square of Earth (about 25,000 land squares) against a Moon or Mars site on slope, local relief, landform shape, surface temperature and albedo, using open NASA, USGS and NOAA data. For each place, the app shows where the analogy is strong, where it breaks down, and what the place is good or not good for. A gap map shows which parts of the Moon and Mars Earth cannot match, so teams know which tests need a thermal chamber or a vacuum chamber instead of a field trip. Every number names its source, and missing data is shown as “No sourced value”, never guessed.
details:
What it does. You fly between Earth, the Moon and Mars. You click a candidate site, or any point on the surface, and press “Find on Earth”. The app scores every Earth square against that point and paints the best matches on the globe. For each match it shows the country and province, its rank among all of Earth (“top 0.1% of Earth”), and a plain summary: Strong analogy, Partial, Breaks down, Use it for, Not for. You can pick a question (Rover mobility, Landing hazard, Thermal cycling) so that only the measurements that matter for it are used. “Copy this report as text” gives a written analog report with values, rank, limits and sources. We compare five named Moon and Mars sites (Shackleton, Tranquility Base, Jezero, Olympus Mons, Valles Marineris) with 18 named Earth sites. A GIS view maps, for every point on the Moon and Mars, the best match Earth can reach. A Method panel shows the formula, every source, and a backtest of where known analog pairs rank. A Base plan tool places a habitat, solar field, landing pad and roads on real terrain from your inputs.

How it works. A Python pipeline reads the raw data and builds a 1° Earth grid and 111 km patches around Moon and Mars points. For each measurement, similarity = 1 − |difference| ÷ scale, never below 0. Measurements are grouped into terrain, landform, thermal and albedo, and each group counts equally. The match is the average. The scales and the 80%/60% strong/breaks-down bands are our own rule of thumb, and the app says so.

Data. NOAA ETOPO 2022 (Earth height), NASA MODIS (Earth temperature and albedo), WorldClim 2.1 (air temperature), USGS LRO LOLA and NASA LRO Diviner (Moon height and temperature), USGS MOLA-HRSC and NASA MGS TES (Mars height, temperature, albedo), NASA PGDA product 90 (Shackleton).

Benefits and impact. Analog sites are picked from evidence. Teams see in advance which tests Earth can support and which it cannot, which saves time and money and makes test plans easier to defend. Students can explore real mission data and read why places match or do not. The tool also corrects assumptions: for example, Mauna Loa, a classic Moon analog, ranks in the bottom 2% of Earth for Tranquility Base on measured terrain.

Creativity. Most analog work starts from famous sites. We start from measurements and look beyond well-known sites, and we map the opposite question: where Earth fails. The app explains every score, including why it is not higher, and it states its own limits.

What we considered. Multiple dimensions rather than looks alone, scale (111 km squares average small features away), and the things Earth cannot copy: low gravity, vacuum, radiation and thin CO₂ air. Mars temperature exists at only three sites, and the Moon has no albedo map we trust, so those features are left out rather than invented.

Tools. Vanilla JavaScript, HTML and CSS, three.js (r128) for the 3D globes, Python for the data pipeline, GIS rasters, GitHub for the code, Vercel for hosting, and an AI coding assistants to help write and test code. No special hardware.
